newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian police to screen party election plans.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian police to screen party election plans.

text.p: Indonesian police will screen the campaign plans of the country's three officially approved parties before the May 29 general election, the Jakarta Post newspaper reported on Saturday.
Brigadier-General Nurfaizi, the national police spokesman, was quoted as saying each party had to submit their plans to police to obtain a letter of reference to conduct campaigning.
"Campaigners should tell police the theme of the campaign, the campaign aids they are going to use, the numbers of participants and the place where the campaign will be held," Nurfaizi said.
He said the three parties should submit details to police at least seven days prior to the campaign start so police could help maintain order and ensure the safety of campaigners.

Last week, the government tightened its grip on political activity ahead of the polls with the release of guidelines restricting public gatherings before the election and ensuring the vetting of all speeches broadcast on radio and television during the campaign.

The government has previously issued regulations to put an end to large outdoor rallies that were a prominent feature of the last election campaign and often included entertainment from local artists.
Campaigning for the 425 seats in the 500 seat parliament is restricted to a 25-day period between April 29 and May 23.
A five-day cooling-off period separates campaigning and polling day. Armed forces members do not vote and receive 75 seats in the parliament.

Authorities have said they fear any large election gatherings could lead to violent outbreaks after a number of riots in recent months across the country, triggered by economic, ethnic and religious tensions.
The three legal parties are the ruling Golkar, the minority non-government Moslem-based United Development Party (PPP) and the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI).
Analysts say the restrictions favour Golkar, which captured around 68 percent of the vote at the last election and which targets a 70 percent share at the 1997 poll.
The PPP won 17 percent of the vote in 1997 and the PDI 15 percent.
All candidates for the poll have been screened by the government and the security forces.
